\CRchapter{19}{The First Planting Week}{Days 91–93 · Seed 2–4, Y.H. 813}{Low Kiln, Sill}
\CRepigraph{Sow with the hand and count with the hand; the slate lies in the sun and takes no seed. A strip is a direction until somebody puts a back into it, and a direction has no figure to be entered.}{A saying of the seed-grounds east of Low Kiln}

\begin{CRchronicle}{19}
On the second day of Seed the work went east of Low Kiln onto the strips the boy had carried for a month only as a direction. Brooms went around what the sweep had left; seed came out of a fist in handfuls nobody counted, and nobody put a figure to hands or strips. Berr Clay came down with his office cord folded under his coat, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, and told the yard a number goes into a slate, not a strip, that the levy was called but not by him.

At the well Sella Vail left the empty place at the row’s end with no figure and told a woman to ask the pot what a wet thing costs; the house had said it. She gave the bucket its instruction before the women and never to the basket. The boy kept ninety-one exactly against the house’s loaves and glances.

On Thirdday Jorra Vail came through the finger’s-width-open door with grey dust past his bent finger, told the wheel it cared only for steady hands, and put that finger into the damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence. He read the damper as the bite that holds a vessel whole and can take a hand off a man, with no Grathic word for both. Tarn set his knife on its sill with six years counted and the seventh held, told the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, and swept his broom over the collector’s road without turning. No collector came.

At the Fishstairs Mira Silt answered a question about the run with \emph{Ask the river} and put her thumb under her apron to the grey cord when a buyer named a figure, shifting a creel to show the second twisted twice beneath it, neither knot counted and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. The steps came back four, four and a landing out of line that a market walked over without a fall; word came that the weak board at the Weir was gone or trodden flat and nobody had gone down to see which. The soft-cuffed clerk still sat for a measure nobody had called.

Three doors down Alda Reed laid her birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold, crossed two fingers at the birth-flower before she knew it and covered the sign with a dead woman’s date. \emph{Warm and breathing, that’s all I’ve set down}, she said, exact and not true. Her tin stayed shut; her sixth slate stayed face-down, six pages unread. At dusk Sella set him on his bed, put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen. The river’s note came through the door and the fire’s gap through the floor, in two places. He was ninety-three days old; nobody had told him so. His hand went up an inch toward the water and came down. Nothing had been joined, paid, explained or ended.
\end{CRchronicle}
